habitat: The common hippopotamus inhabits rivers, lakes, and swamps throughout sub-Saharan Africa, from South Africa north to Sudan, Ethiopia, and west to Senegal. They require permanent bodies of water deep enough for complete submersion — at least 1.5-2 meters — with adjacent grasslands for grazing. Hippos spend daylight hours submerged or wallowing in water to keep their massive bodies cool and prevent sunburn. At night, they emerge to graze, traveling up to 10 kilometers from water.
diet: Hippopotamuses are primarily herbivorous, grazing on short grasses during nighttime excursions. An adult hippo consumes 40-50 kg of grass per night — relatively modest for their enormous size of 1,500-3,200 kg, reflecting their low metabolic rate. They use their massive, muscular lips — up to 50 cm wide — to crop grass close to the ground. Though primarily herbivorous, hippos have been occasionally observed scavenging carcasses or preying on small animals, suggesting opportunistic omnivory.
behavior: Hippopotamuses are highly social, living in pods of 10-30 individuals dominated by a territorial bull. Bulls defend stretches of river through dramatic displays: yawning widely to show massive canines (up to 50 cm), splashing, and vocalizing with deep, resonant honks and bellows audible above and below water simultaneously. Hippos cannot swim — they walk or bounce along the bottom. Fights between bulls can be lethal. Females give birth to a single calf in the water, which nurses underwater. Despite their rotund appearance, hippos can run at 30 km/h on land and are responsible for more human fatalities in Africa than any other large mammal.
facts: Hippopotamuses are the third-largest land mammal after elephants and rhinoceroses. Despite their pig-like appearance, their closest living relatives are cetaceans (whales and dolphins). They secrete a red, oily substance called 'blood sweat' — actually a combination of sunscreening and antibiotic compounds. Hippos can hold their breath for 5 minutes and sleep underwater, surfacing to breathe reflexively without waking. Their powerful jaws can bite with 1,800 PSI, crushing crocodiles. Wild populations number approximately 125,000-150,000.
naming: Hippo-themed names might reflect their massive size, African origin, or semi-aquatic lifestyle. Consider names like Hippo, Tank, Bubbles (ironic), Nile, Zambezi, Brutus, Hulk, Splash, Giza, Kongo, or Jumbo.
